$$
\int \frac{\sec^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\tan{\left(x \right)} + 2}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

Choose the antiderivative. In each choice, $C$ is an arbitrary constant."] [:db/add "bed2914b-3819-5048-a75d-3b7c824e58d5" :question/worked-solution "Let $u=\tan{\left(x \right)} + 2$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=\sec^{2}{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Including the differential factor gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int \frac{\sec^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\tan{\left(x \right)} + 2}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the integration rule:

$$
\int 1/u\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C.
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
\ln\left|\tan{\left(x \right)} + 2\right|+C.
$$"] [:db/add "bed2914b-3819-5048-a75d-3b7c824e58d5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [:db/add "bed2914b-3819-5048-a75d-3b7c824e58d5" :question/answer-fields $$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \sin{\left(x \right)}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int \frac{3 \sin{\left(x \right)}}{\cos{\left(x \right)} + 2}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=-3\left(\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Use the integration rule:

$$
\int 1/u\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C.
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
-3\left(\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u\right)=-3\left(\ln\left|u\right|\right)+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
- 3 \ln\left|\cos{\left(x \right)} + 2\right|+C.

$$

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=\tan{\left(x \right)} \sec{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Including the differential factor gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int \frac{3 \tan{\left(x \right)} \sec{\left(x \right)}}{\sec{\left(x \right)} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=3\left(\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Use the integration rule:

$$
\int 1/u\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C.
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
3\left(\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u\right)=3\left(\ln\left|u\right|\right)+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
3 \ln\left|\sec{\left(x \right)} + 1\right|+C.
$$"] [:db/add "e578efee-eae6-51b9-a40e-d230ab113937" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [:db/add "e578efee-eae6-51b9-a40e-d230ab113937" :question/answer-fields $$

$$

$$
\int 1/u\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C.

$$
- \frac{1}{2}\left(\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u\right)=- \frac{1}{2}\left(\ln\left|u\right|\right)+C.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=\tan{\left(x \right)} \sec{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Including the differential factor gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int \frac{3 \tan{\left(x \right)} \sec{\left(x \right)}}{\sec{\left(x \right)} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=3\left(\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Use the integration rule:

$$
\int 1/u\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C.
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
3\left(\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u\right)=3\left(\ln\left|u\right|\right)+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
3 \ln\left|\sec{\left(x \right)} + 1\right|+C.
$$"] ["e578efee-eae6-51b9-a40e-d230ab113937" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["e578efee-eae6-51b9-a40e-d230ab113937" :question/answer-fields "679fc75c-be91-5eb4-8094-bd79a74184e2"] question.:question/problem:
Find an antiderivative.

$$
\int \frac{\sec^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\tan{\left(x \right)} + 2}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

Choose the antiderivative. In each choice, $C$ is an arbitrary constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=\tan{\left(x \right)} + 2$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=\sec^{2}{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Including the differential factor gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int \frac{\sec^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\tan{\left(x \right)} + 2}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the integration rule:

$$
\int 1/u\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C.
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
\ln\left|\tan{\left(x \right)} + 2\right|+C.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate exactly.

$$
\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{2 \sin{\left(x \right)} \cos{\left(x \right)}}{\sin^{2}{\left(x \right)} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

{{answer}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=\sin^{2}{\left(x \right)} + 1$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=2 \sin{\left(x \right)} \cos{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Transform both bounds:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=0&\Longrightarrow u=1\\x=\frac{\pi}{2}&\Longrightarrow u=2\end{aligned}
$$

Including the differential factor gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{2 \sin{\left(x \right)} \cos{\left(x \right)}}{\sin^{2}{\left(x \right)} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=\int_{1}^{2} \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the integration rule:

$$
\int 1/u\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C.
$$

Endpoint values: $\sin{\left(0 \right)}=0,\quad \sin{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}=1$.

Both transformed bounds are positive. Evaluating gives

$$
\left[\ln u\right]_{1}^{2}=\ln\left(2\right)-\ln\left(1\right).
$$

The answer is

$$
\ln\left(2\right)-\ln\left(1\right).
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate exactly.

$$
\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{3 \sin{\left(x \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\cos^{3}{\left(x \right)} + 2}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

{{answer}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=\cos^{3}{\left(x \right)} + 2$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=- 3 \sin{\left(x \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Transform both bounds:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=0&\Longrightarrow u=3\\x=\frac{\pi}{2}&\Longrightarrow u=2\end{aligned}
$$

The new bounds decrease. Keep this order when evaluating the antiderivative.

Including the differential factor gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{3 \sin{\left(x \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\cos^{3}{\left(x \right)} + 2}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=-\left(\int_{3}^{2} \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Use the integration rule:

$$
\int 1/u\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C.
$$

Endpoint values: $\cos{\left(0 \right)}=1,\quad \cos{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}=0$.

Both transformed bounds are positive. Evaluating gives

$$
-\left(\left[\ln u\right]_{3}^{2}\right)=-\left(\ln\left(2\right)-\ln\left(3\right)\right).
$$

The answer is

$$
-\left(\ln\left(2\right)-\ln\left(3\right)\right).
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find an antiderivative.

$$
\int \frac{2 x \sec^{2}{\left(x^{2} \right)}}{\tan{\left(x^{2} \right)} + 2}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

{{answer}} $+C$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=\tan{\left(x^{2} \right)} + 2$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=2 x \sec^{2}{\left(x^{2} \right)}.
$$

Including the differential factor gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int \frac{2 x \sec^{2}{\left(x^{2} \right)}}{\tan{\left(x^{2} \right)} + 2}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the integration rule:

$$
\int 1/u\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C.
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
\ln\left|\tan{\left(x^{2} \right)} + 2\right|+C.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find an antiderivative.

$$
\int \frac{\tan{\left(x \right)} \sec^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\sec{\left(x \right)} + 3}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

{{answer}} $+C$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=\sec{\left(x \right)} + 3$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=\tan{\left(x \right)} \sec{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Since $\sec{\left(x \right)}=u-3$, rewrite the remaining factor:

$$
\frac{u-3}{u}=1-\frac{3}{u}.
$$

Including the differential factor gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int \frac{\tan{\left(x \right)} \sec^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\sec{\left(x \right)} + 3}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=\int 1 - \frac{3}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the integration rule:

$$
\int 1/u\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C.
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
\int 1 - \frac{3}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u=u-3\left(\ln\left|u\right|\right)+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
\sec{\left(x \right)} + 3-3\left(\ln\left|\sec{\left(x \right)} + 3\right|\right)+C.
$$
